--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.transitive_reduction()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Compute the transitive reduction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.transitive_reduction()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Compute the transitive reduction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). title: >- [Graph.transitive_reduction()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Compute the transitive reduction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the transitive reduction of a directed acyclic graph (DAG). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L77115-L77240){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.transitive_reduction() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Transitive reduction](../assets/graphs/transitive-reduction.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A DAG on A, B, C, D: the chain A to B to C to D plus three shortcut arrows A to C, B to D and A to D, in the accent color. The reduction drops the shortcuts, shown dashed, because the chain already reaches the same nodes." width="100%"} The transitive reduction is the minimal subgraph that maintains the same reachability as the original graph. It removes redundant edges while preserving all path relationships. If there's a path from `A` to `C` via `B`, the direct edge `A -> C` (if it exists) is redundant and will be removed. This method only works on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). Cyclic graphs do not have a unique transitive reduction. Time complexity: `O(V × E)` where `V` is nodes and `E` is edges Space complexity: `O(V + E)` ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : New directed graph representing the transitive reduction. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If called on an undirected graph or a graph containing cycles. ::: ## Common Use Cases {.doc-common-use-cases} - simplifying dependency graphs to show only direct dependencies - reducing storage for reachability queries - visualizing the minimal structure of a DAG - cleaning up inferred relationships ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The transitive reduction of a DAG is *unique* (Aho, Garey, and Ullman, 1972): among all subgraphs with the same reachability, exactly one attains the minimum edge count, and this call returns that graph. Uniqueness fails for cyclic graphs (any edge on a cycle can be removed without losing reachability), so the implementation raises `ValueError` on cyclic input rather than picking an arbitrary reduction. The construction runs in $O(V \cdot E)$ time and $O(V + E)$ space. Reductions are especially useful for visualizing the essential dependency structure of a DAG without the visual clutter of edges implied by transitivity. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~transitive_closure`) : Every edge with the same reachability. [](`~topological_sort`) : Order the nodes so that every edge points forward. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The reduction drops the arrow from `A` to `C`, since `A` already reaches `C` through `B`: ::: {#89516a76 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "C")], directed=True ) reduced = graph.transitive_reduction() reduced.count_edges(), reduced.has_edge("A", "C") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, False) ``` ::: ::: ### A redundant prerequisite `courses()` holds the courses of a made-up computer science program, with an arrow from each course to every course that requires it. CS201 lists CS101 as a prerequisite, but it also requires CS102, which requires CS101. The reduction drops that one arrow, and the order in which courses can be taken doesn't change: ::: {#af2cd640 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} courses = ec.courses() reduced = courses.transitive_reduction() ( courses.count_edges(), reduced.count_edges(), reduced.has_edge("CS101", "CS201"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (19, 18, False) ``` ::: ::: The program on the left, with the redundant arrow picked out, and its reduction on the right, drawn in the same place: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#d89f4e87 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} stages = dict(enumerate(courses.topological_generations())) courses.layout_multipartite(subset_key=stages) reduced.set_node_attrs("pos", courses.get_node_attrs("pos")) courses.plot( layout="pos", highlight=[("CS101", "CS201")], label_by="label", width=320, height=320, legend=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#07f07642 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} reduced.plot( layout="pos", label_by="label", width=320, height=320, legend=False ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: So the two chains of prerequisites from CS101 to CS460 become one: ::: {#83dcec51 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} len(courses.all_simple_paths("CS101", "CS460")), len( reduced.all_simple_paths("CS101", "CS460") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (2, 1) ``` ::: ::: [Directed acyclic graphs](../user-guide/dags.qmd#closure-and-reduction) removes the redundant dependencies from the plan for a house.
